title: Probability distributions: choose by the question
summary: Distinguish counts, waiting times, proportions, tails and multivariate models.

sections.heading: Discrete outcomes
sections.body: A Bernoulli variable represents a binary outcome with success probability p. A binomial variable counts successes in n independent trials with the same p. A categorical distribution selects one of several categories; a multinomial counts category outcomes over repeated trials. A degenerate distribution places all probability at one value.

sections.heading: Counts, waiting and sampling
sections.body: Poisson models count events under a specified rate model. Geometric distributions describe trials until a first success, with conventions differing on whether the successful trial is counted; negative binomial distributions extend the waiting-to-success idea. Hypergeometric models sampling without replacement. Wallenius’ noncentral hypergeometric distribution introduces biased sampling. Yule–Simon and zeta/Zipf models describe particular discrete heavy-tailed patterns.

sections.heading: Symmetric and bounded values
sections.body: A normal distribution is specified by a mean and variance. A uniform distribution assigns equal density over an interval. Beta and Kumaraswamy distributions describe flexible shapes on a bounded interval, commonly (0,1). A triangular distribution adds a mode between endpoints; a trapezoidal distribution has a flat central density region. A Laplace distribution has an exponential-shaped tail on either side of its center.

sections.heading: Positive values and waiting times
sections.body: The exponential distribution has a constant hazard and is memoryless. Weibull models can have increasing or decreasing hazard. Lognormal variables have normally distributed logarithms. Inverse Gaussian, Gompertz and Lindley distributions are other positive-variable families; suitability depends on the generating process and fit, not simply positive observations. Folded normal and half-normal distributions arise from absolute values of normal variables.

sections.heading: Heavy tails and extremes
sections.body: Cauchy is a heavy-tailed distribution whose mean and variance are undefined. Lévy, Pareto, stable, Burr and Fisk families provide different tail behavior. Generalized extreme-value models describe certain normalized maxima, and generalized error and Tukey lambda families allow flexible shapes. A power law is a functional tail pattern, not a universal explanation for a dataset.

sections.heading: Multiple dimensions and angles
sections.body: Bivariate and multivariate normal models describe joint variation. Dirichlet distributions model vectors of proportions; Wishart distributions are associated with covariance matrices. Von Mises and Kent distributions describe directional data in different spaces. Rayleigh, Rician and Nakagami models appear in magnitude and signal applications.

sections.heading: Families versus descriptions
sections.body: Skewed, symmetric, unimodal, bimodal, multimodal, long-tailed and U-shaped describe properties rather than identifying a unique distribution. A marginal comes from a joint distribution; a mixture combines component distributions. Truncation restricts support and requires renormalization. An empirical distribution assigns mass to observed data.

sections.heading: A count example
sections.body: If X is binomial with n = 3 and p = 0.5, then P(X=2) = C(3,2)×0.5²×0.5 = 3/8. This calculation requires independent trials with a common success probability.

sections.heading: Ambiguous names in the collection
sections.body: The labels “T Factorial”, “F J Shaped”, “G-and-H”, “Normal Lindley” and “Open Ended” need a precise definition or original reference before a formula can be assigned. “Inverse normal” may mean a quantile function or a named distribution depending on context; it should not automatically be equated with inverse Gaussian. These unresolved labels are retained in the editorial inventory.

title: Regression: fit, interpret and diagnose
summary: Move beyond fitting a line to checking assumptions, coding variables and measuring errors.

sections.heading: A complete line example
sections.body: For x = [0,1,2] and observed y = [1,2,2], the least-squares line is ŷ = 7/6 + x/2. Fitted values are [7/6,5/3,13/6] and residuals y−ŷ are [−1/6,1/3,−1/6]. Their squared sum is 1/6.

sections.heading: Separate error measures
sections.body: RMSE is √(SSE/n), approximately 0.2357 here. Residual standard error for this line with an intercept and slope is √(SSE/(n−2)), approximately 0.4082. They use different denominators. R² = 1−SSE/SST measures improvement over the mean baseline in this setting; out-of-sample R² can be negative.

sections.heading: Code features deliberately
sections.body: One-hot encoding represents categories with indicators. In an intercept-based linear model, a reference category or other constraint avoids redundant columns. Deviation coding compares levels with an overall effect under a defined convention. An interaction term lets one predictor’s association depend on another; a main effect is not a claim of independence.

sections.heading: Check stability and assumptions
sections.body: Collinear predictors can make coefficients unstable. Leverage concerns an observation’s predictor position, while influence concerns its effect on the fitted model. Examine residual patterns, changing variance (heteroskedasticity), dependence and unusual observations. Normality assumptions relate to particular inferential procedures, not a universal prerequisite for prediction.

sections.heading: Extend the model
sections.body: Polynomial terms and splines represent curves; knots locate spline transitions. Generalized additive models combine smooth effects. Lasso penalizes coefficient magnitudes, Bayesian regression uses a prior, quantile regression targets conditional quantiles, and robust regression reduces sensitivity under chosen loss rules. These approaches answer different questions.

sections.heading: Validate outside the fitting data
sections.body: Cross-validation rotates training and validation folds, but the split must respect groups and time. Fit scaling and feature selection within the training portion. Use weighted regression only when the weight meaning is justified.

title: Experiments, uncertainty and evaluation formulas
summary: Work through a confusion matrix, sampling uncertainty and the logic of testing.

sections.heading: Calculate a confusion matrix
sections.body: Suppose TP=8, FP=2, FN=4 and TN=86. Accuracy is 94/100 = 94%; precision is 8/10 = 80%; recall is 8/12 ≈ 66.7%; specificity is 86/88 ≈ 97.7%. F1 = 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN) = 16/22 ≈ 72.7%. The same model can look strong or weak depending on the error that matters.

sections.heading: Change the threshold
sections.body: A threshold converts a score into a decision. ROC plots true-positive rate against false-positive rate across thresholds; a precision–recall curve focuses on predicted and actual positives. AUC summarizes a curve and does not choose the right operating threshold for a business.

sections.heading: Sampling uncertainty
sections.body: For independent observations with sample standard deviation s, the estimated standard error of the mean is s/√n. A central limit theorem can justify an approximation under its conditions; it does not make the original observations normally distributed. Bootstrap resampling draws samples with replacement from observed data and has its own limitations.

sections.heading: Design the comparison
sections.body: Random assignment allocates subjects to treatment and control; random sampling selects observations from a population. They solve different problems. Define effect size, statistical power and the analysis before examining results where possible.

sections.heading: Choose an appropriate test
sections.body: A t-test concerns means under specified assumptions; ANOVA compares modelled group effects using an F statistic. Chi-square procedures can compare categorical counts, and permutation tests use an exchangeability argument. Pairwise and omnibus tests answer different questions.

sections.heading: Interpret errors and multiple tests
sections.body: A Type I error rejects a true null; a Type II error fails to reject a false null under an alternative. Alpha controls a test’s Type I error rate under its assumptions. False discovery rate concerns the expected proportion of false rejections among rejections, with conventions for no rejections. Multiple testing needs an appropriate procedure rather than reusing an unadjusted threshold.

title: Search and optimization methods: a field guide
summary: Understand the mechanism behind search methods and distinguish algorithm names from settings.

sections.heading: Gradient and curvature methods
sections.body: BFGS is a quasi-Newton method that builds a curvature approximation. Rprop uses gradient signs to adapt update steps; momentum carries a running influence of previous gradients. KKT conditions combine stationarity, feasibility and complementary slackness under specified conditions; they are not a blanket proof of global optimality.

sections.heading: Evolutionary search
sections.body: Genetic algorithms select, recombine and mutate candidate representations. Genetic programming evolves program structures. Differential evolution perturbs candidates using differences between population members. Estimation-of-distribution algorithms learn a probabilistic model of promising candidates and sample from it.

sections.heading: Collective search
sections.body: Particle swarm optimization updates candidate positions using individual and collective information. Ant-colony methods maintain pheromone-like search information, often for combinatorial problems. Artificial bee colony and the bees algorithm allocate exploration among candidate regions; they are distinct methods despite similar metaphors.

sections.heading: Memory and neighborhoods
sections.body: Tabu search uses memory to restrict selected moves. Variable neighborhood search changes neighborhood structures to escape local patterns. Simulated annealing can accept worse candidates according to a temperature schedule. Shuffled frog leaping combines local improvement with regrouping of candidates.

sections.heading: Other named metaheuristics
sections.body: Cuckoo search, firefly algorithms, gravitational search, imperialist competition and cultural algorithms define different population-update mechanisms. Their biological or social metaphors do not establish performance. Compare a specific implementation with simple baselines under the same evaluation budget.

sections.heading: Harmony search settings
sections.body: Harmony search builds candidates using stored solutions, random choices and adjustments. Harmony memory considering rate is commonly a parameter governing memory use; it should not be listed as a standalone optimizer. The source’s “Harmony Memory Upgrade” label needs an original reference to establish its intended meaning.

sections.heading: A fair comparison
sections.body: State the objective, constraints, variable encoding, stopping rule, random seeds and compute budget. Run multiple trials for stochastic methods and report distributions of outcomes, not only the best run.

title: Image features: edges, corners, blobs and descriptors
summary: Organize classical computer-vision methods by what they detect or describe.

sections.heading: Edges and derivatives
sections.body: Sobel, Prewitt and Roberts operators approximate image derivatives. Canny combines smoothing, gradient information and further processing to produce edges. Deriche filters offer another approach. An edge marks an intensity change, which need not coincide with an object boundary.

sections.heading: Corners and local structure
sections.body: Harris and Shi–Tomasi use local gradient structure to identify informative points. A structure tensor summarizes variation in different directions; points with variation in more than one direction can be useful for tracking and matching.

sections.heading: Scale and regions
sections.body: Laplacian-of-Gaussian, Difference-of-Gaussians and Hessian-based methods detect structures over scale. Maximally stable extremal regions identify stable image regions across thresholds. Image pyramids support multiscale processing. Scale-space methods explain how representations change with smoothing.

sections.heading: Shapes and invariance
sections.body: Hough transforms accumulate evidence for parameterized shapes; a generalized Hough transform handles more general templates. Affine-adapted region methods aim to improve matching under viewpoint changes. These methods have assumptions and can fail under occlusion, noise or repeated textures.

sections.heading: Descriptors
sections.body: SIFT, SURF and GLOH summarize local visual structure for comparison. HOG describes gradient orientations, local binary patterns encode local intensity comparisons, and GIST summarizes scene-level structure. A descriptor is different from a detector: one describes a region while the other finds candidate regions.

sections.heading: Choose by the task
sections.body: Tracking, image matching, classification and segmentation need different outputs. Evaluate repeatability, robustness, compute cost and any licensing or patent constraints for the intended implementation. The source’s PCBR abbreviation requires its original reference before a specific algorithm can be described.

title: Business analytics and scenario planning
summary: Distinguish describing results, predicting outcomes and exploring uncertain futures.

sections.heading: Start with the decision
sections.body: Aggregate analysis summarizes populations or segments; trend analysis follows change over time; segmentation groups cases for a stated purpose. A descriptive relationship does not prove what will happen if a business intervenes.

sections.heading: Estimate with transparent assumptions
sections.body: For a hypothetical market with 10,000 eligible customers, 20% adoption and 50 units of annual revenue per adopter, the estimate is 100,000 units. If adoption ranges from 10% to 30%, the result ranges from 50,000 to 150,000. These are scenario assumptions, not observed outcomes.

sections.heading: Triangulate
sections.body: Approach an estimate using another model or independent evidence. Agreement is more useful when the methods do not share the same hidden assumptions. Record uncertainty in the inputs instead of disguising it with precise output formatting.

sections.heading: Map plausible futures
sections.body: Scenario planning examines multiple plausible futures rather than assigning certainty to one forecast. Cognitive maps represent perceived relationships; fuzzy cognitive maps add weighted influences and update rules. Their results depend on elicitation, weights and assumptions.

sections.heading: Use experts carefully
sections.body: Delphi-style exercises gather and revise expert judgments; scenario workshops can incorporate stakeholder perspectives and identify disagreements. The source’s specific scenario counts and expert-count recommendations lack cited evidence and are not treated as fixed requirements.

sections.heading: Close the loop
sections.body: State the decision, monitor signals that distinguish scenarios and revise assumptions as evidence arrives. A useful scenario changes what the team is prepared to do, rather than only producing a presentation.
